utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did he ask you to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He to go back to a detail found in your statement, and we are now going back to 1998, whereby you describe the operation carried out by your unit on the road leading towards Rakovina. In your statement you say that the operation took three days. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, if I can remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I reminded you that you said for the transcript that you spent at least two nights in the field on that road, would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that after an additional check you said that on the 3rd you were already at your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 3rd I set out from the barracks to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I waited for a convoy. I don't know exactly, but I waited most of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You waited for a convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were in the barracks waiting for a convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And before that you explained to us that it took you quite a long time to go back to the barracks because of the tank that had broken down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you were almost half a day and one entire night on the road with that tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was around 3.00 in the morning, 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. When we reached Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And how long did you wait for the rest of the convoy to come back to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't wait. We went together in a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us assume then -- let's deal with this this way. You reached the barracks at 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the barracks to go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the next day -- well, it was a long time ago. I don't know whether it was that day or the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's try to deal with it this way. Do you remember when, on what day, you reached your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was on the same day. I came home the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It could be either the 3rd or the 4th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said the 3rd or the 4th. I cannot remember exactly. It was a long time ago. I think it was the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I told you that the operation concerning Rakovina began on the 2nd, at 6.00 a.m., would that tally with what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How come you then say you spent two days in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we got there before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did you find the infantry there, who had spent two days in the woods before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the first day when we arrived. We were there for two days. We spent one night there and then the next night we reached the barracks. I count that as two days and two nights for the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to something else, then. You said you didn't know that General Delic testified before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he testified, but I didn't listen to his testimony. But I heard that he was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you came here, when you were being proofed for this testimony, were you shown parts of General Delic's statement concerning your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No? And you were not shown or told that General Delic identified a different house that was fired at from the tank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he did so as to try and protect Milosevic. Whatever he said was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there is a chicken farm in the village of Beci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you shown maps showing the position of your unit and your position during the operation in Jeskovo and the one pertaining to Rakovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, if I was shown?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP show you certain maps or military maps indicating unit positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you say you left Kosovo on the 6th of June. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, six days before the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: After that, did you go back to serve the rest of your military term?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's not in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what was the remainder of your military term?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How did it happen that you went home on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Home?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got a weekend off from the army. Everyone had one before that, and I insisted that I be given one as a reward. And it was a long weekend; it lasted for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you supposed to go back to your unit after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a testimony before this Tribunal, and this is the Milosevic transcript, page 42238, in which it was said --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I believe we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness K54.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The good news is that I'm the last person to put questions to you, but I do have a number of them. I would kindly ask you to focus on the part of your statement which speaks about the police and the PJP, since that particular area is of the most interest to me. Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go to page 4, paragraph 2. In the English it is page 3, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just count from the top of the page, page 4, paragraph 2, the second paragraph. What is mentioned there is the area of Djakovica, and you say: "We went to another village which was about 3 to 5 kilometres away. That village was empty of any civilians. There was a PJP unit from Djakovica there and some police in normal plain blue uniforms." The policemen in blue uniforms, did they participate in the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say: "During that night a firefight started between the PJP and someone in the force."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not during that night. It was just getting dark, just before it got dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. "I could not see who was firing in our direction, but we assumed that it was the KLA terrorists." Then you mention the policeman who was shot and fell down. You say you don't know whether he was dead. And in the next paragraph you explain that on the third day infantry came out of the forest and that you were ordered to give them water, and that they said they had covered only 3 to 5 kilometres. The reason for that, was it because they encountered KLA resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been some.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say they returned just before it got dark that evening and that you were ordered to line up and head back for the barracks in Prizren. The PJP remained behind. "The following day I went home on leave." In the two paragraphs you talk about combat, about fighting against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe about one fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your words, the villagers had left the villages and they were not there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there were no executions during that fighting, since there were no civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no executions, but we set the houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't know whether there had been any fighting there prior to your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which PJP units participated in those actions at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just know their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When your guys returned from the field, you went to the barracks in Prizren; therefore, you don't know what the PJP were involved in at that location after the operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 5 now, the fifth paragraph, and in the English version it's page 5, the first paragraph. My colleagues have already asked you about this, about the village of Jeskovo, and what was put to you was that a report was written about this incident of the KVM, that is to say the OSCE monitoring mission. You describe a man who went out of the cellar with his hands up, saying: "I surrender, I surrender." You say that you were present there and you describe what happened by saying that two members of the PJP grabbed this man, one of them pulled out a knife and cut off both the ears of the man that had surrendered. And then, in your words, they killed him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't right there directly to see that they cut off his ears, and I didn't see -- I wasn't there when they just grabbed him. But I was so nearby that one could establish straight away what it was that had happened to him. Other soldiers saw this, so they added on to what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you compiled a story that you heard from others in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I saw that the man didn't have any ears and that he had been killed. Perhaps two, three minutes, let's say five minutes in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He got out of the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the documentation we have, we established that what you spoke of occurred on the 11th of March, 1999, around 1430 hours. I'm referring to the action that was observed by the verification mission. First of all, at that moment did you know that the Kosovo Verification Mission had approved of this operation and supervised it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not aware of that, but they certainly didn't supervise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not in a single document that was compiled during and after this operation has it been documented that any of the persons killed did not have any ears. Can we agree on that, and you just sounded rather uncertain yourself about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I just saw this man without any ears. Well, as he fell, I'm not sure about the other ear but I saw that he certainly didn't have one ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now I would like us to move on to the fourth paragraph on page 5. It's the same one, isn't it, it's the same paragraph in the English text, too. You say: "I personally saw seven bodies, but it made me sick and I did not want to see any others. I later heard that the PJP returned the next day to clear up the bodies and they confirmed that there were 30 terrorists killed during that attack." In your view, is it the task of the PJP to collect bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many people got killed on the KLA side in this fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To who was it that the PJP confirmed that there were 30 terrorists killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't say who -- you don't know who the -- who said so from the PJP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about it in the barracks allegedly, that there were 30 of them, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In your statement dated the 16th of July, 2002, you talk about documents being taken away. Did you ever take anybody's personal documents away from them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever order you to take documents away from people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the transcript yesterday on page 10512, line 3, you say that a soldier told you that documents were being taken away at the Vrmice border crossing, that's what it says here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vrbnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I thought, that it was Vrbnica? Do you know the name of the soldier who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that soldier claim that he was at the border crossing as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question and we will be done. Yesterday -- well, sometimes it happens due to interpretation as well, the transcript said that you were receiving warnings or threats from Serbian policemen. Is it Serbian policemen or Montenegrin policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness K54. No further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, just a couple of questions. How old were you in 1998, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in 1976, so 20 I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And before you started your training, your short military training, did you know anything about the structure of the VJ, the different units, what was a brigade, a battalion, a combat group, whatever? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just knew the names sort of brigade, battalion, company. As for the meaning, I didn't know very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And during these six weeks of training, did you receive any information, more detailed information on all these things, the structure of the VJ, all the details, what was what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, six weeks is the information that we were given here, six weeks of training. I don't think that's what the witness said in his examination-in-chief or in the re-direct. Two and a half months is ten weeks. I really don't know why the witness is being led this way in re-direct. Another leading question was when it was said "during your training." During this fast-track training, short military training. I don't think that that is the proper way to examine a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I misspoke. I meant ten weeks or two and a half months. I did not have my math right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But I think the question was answered -- no, actually, it wasn't. I'm sorry. So I repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: During the two and a half months of military training before you were sent into Kosovo, did you receive any information on -- detailed information on how the VJ was structured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to the village of Jeskovo. My learned colleagues Mr. Ackerman yesterday, Mr. Bakrac, and Mr. Lukic today all referred to the OSCE being present during this time in this area. Now, did you see the OSCE somewhere in or around Jeskovo during this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked the witness and he explicitly said that he never saw any OSCE representatives in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you don't think that that's a matter that the Prosecution would be entitled to explore in re-examination? If you had asked it before and you were asking it again, the point you are making would apply, but it doesn't apply when someone may be considering a challenge. Let's wait and see where this goes. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, did you see anything of -- did you see the OSCE in or around Jeskovo during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we returned, just one car, near Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that very day that the operation was going on, did you see any OSCE cars or representatives in the very village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. My learned colleague Mr. Bakrac referred to an exhibit 5D112 and he referred to this report, referring to the OSCE patrols being denied access to the area at that time. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. "The OSCE report also states that verifiers observed a heavy bombardment of Jeskovo and reported buildings burning." Would you share this assessment of the situation in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So was there any bombardment of the village that you saw yourself at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. So which part of this assessment do you not share, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessment that I did not notice the OSCE there. How could they write that statement, that allegedly they were there? In that statement that's what they say, but they were not there. But that really means that they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay, but I asked you about if you would disagree with the statement that a heavy bombardment of Jeskovo took place on that day and that houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, that houses were burned, that there was bombardment. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to the seven bodies that you testified you saw in civilian clothes - it was also raised by Mr. Bakrac and some other Defence counsel - do you recall where you saw -- where in the village, in or around the village, you saw these seven bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the village. One I saw in the village, and the others around the village, on some clearings, meadows, by the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when asked about the torching of the house with the towel, by Mr. Bakrac I think, you testified that you also torched a bus and a tractor. Why did you torch these two vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was ordered to torch them. Why? I don't know. Quite simply, to have it destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we shortly go into private session for the name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, there's one last aspect I need to clarify with you. I'm still not clear about one part of your statement, which you were already cross-examined about, and that is on page 6, paragraph 1, of the B/C/S version. If you could look at that again. In the English version, it is page 5, the second paragraph. It's this reference to the village near Novake. When did you actually go to Novake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On military trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think we misunderstood each other. "When" was the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, when. On the 25th, early in the morning. The 25th of March, when the bombing started, we were going through Novake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how long did you say in Novake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly. We just passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And from there on you went, then, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the village of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And before you went to Novake you stayed where, again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First in the barracks and then we left the barracks because of the forthcoming bombing. Below the barracks there was a military outpatient clinic. We spent that night there, and early in the morning we went towards the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you passed through Novake while going on your way, then, down to Trnje. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think that completes my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a very small question to ask. May I ask? Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, you said you saw six bodies. Later we learned that you saw five of them being killed in your -- while you were viewing it. And then later it came that you saw two of the women being killed in your presence and while you could view it. But then again it transpires from your statement that at the time somebody was shooting at them, that moment you didn't see; however, the thing happened in your presence. Did you spot the killers then, who could those be, because it all happened in seconds? Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see the people who killed those persons. I could see those people fall down and I was taken aback. Therefore, I paid no heed to the persons who killed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Were you not curious who could be around? Did you not see even a shadow? Did you not see anybody close by? Did you not like to even look at somebody running away or -- I mean at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were our soldiers around. Even had I tried to look, I would have been -- would not have been able to understand or see who killed them exactly. The soldiers were there, but I didn't see which one or who killed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: When somebody is shooting and you see somebody falling, then you also see somebody in motion with a barrel. I mean, it doesn't happen just something coming out of a man's body hitting somebody else. Did you see any sort of movement? Did you suspect anybody? Are you not trying to tell us who those men may have been, even you identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not trying to avoid telling you, rather I cannot be certain who it was. I know it must have been one of the soldiers. I saw soldiers there, but I don't know who did it. But at that moment you don't think that way. You don't try to look for the killer. You recognise the fact that someone is being killed and you try to take cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could clarify for me which incident you're talking about so that I don't remain uncertain about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, when I saw those two women running across the fields and there was an elderly man with them, at that moment I saw them being killed by a soldier or soldiers, since there was several. I saw those people fall to the ground. They were still alive and in pain. I didn't pay much attention to who fired at them exactly, which soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it was my understanding that you had seen two women killed. Did you also see the elderly man shot or did he escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was killed. He was the first one to get killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do I correctly recollect your evidence as being that these two women were two of the five women that you took to bury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K54, that completes your evidence. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence, and you're now free to leave. But just stay where you are for a moment while we go into closed session to enable you to leave the courtroom and protect your identity.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your next witness, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Hannis will address you with regard to the scheduling, I would like to make an oral application. You invited us yesterday to reconsider filing a motion for reconsideration regarding your decision of the evidence of Witness K82. And we are herewith moving to ask you to reconsider your oral decision of 19th September and the written decision of 3 October 2006 regarding the evidence by Witness K86. We submit that according to the Appeals Chamber ruling, a Trial Chamber may always reconsider a decision and we will ask you in more detail in our written submission, which we will file this afternoon. This oral application is just for you to be on immediate notice, as you requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think your second reference was actually also to K82. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I wanted to say something concerning the statement of the earlier witness, K54, which may have influenced your decision concerning your decision about K86 -- sorry, K82, having in mind that that issue is still open, that is that both statements may be taken into account. First of all, out of today's testimony I concluded that either there was a breach on the part of the OTP concerning their obligation to disclose certain material or there were such major omissions which made it unable for us to conduct our investigations. I'll try to be brief. In the practice so far, we received different material from the OTP, but even with the Albanian witnesses who were victims an effort was made to forward at least sketches or photographs or any other material in addition to the witness concerning a possible testimony. Concerning this witness that -- who testified for two days, the situation was even more drastic. He was there with a professional from the Prosecutor's team, and on that occasion, without delving into the reasons, no effort was made so as to enable us to conduct a proper and adequate investigation. In certain cases, as far as I could understand from the witness's statement, identification was made from the road, the road being 5 to 6 kilometres away from certain locations referred to in the statement, primarily Damjane and potentially Rogovo. Then identification was made impossible for us of any key location or locations from the key points of the statement, and we couldn't identify the victims even on those occasions when the witness would have been able to pin-point the location of the crime or the place where the bodies could be found. On top of that, we are now in a situation in addition to the late disclosure of the statement and the witnesses being scheduled, we are in a situation to have witnesses in a virtual situation stating something and that same witness is unable to identify locations. We cannot obtain any material and we cannot get the witnesses here who told him things about certain crimes who were there with him at the time, apart from several alleged perpetrators he named. If this is to be the standard for this witness and for other witnesses, because I believe they will try to do the same thing, we will actually have two different statements without any factual or material basis. This will effectively unable us to run our checks on whatever apart from the perpetrators named by the OTP. And then again we would get additional unverified statements and we can go cycle by cycle that way. And my learned friend Mr. Bakrac tells me that I should mention that these incidents were not made part of the indictment and we did not focus our investigations on those incidents. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are all points that go to the weight of the evidence and they are all points that you can -- yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I just respond to some of the allegations, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not content -- I mean why --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just to the allegation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just sit down. Sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If I want to hear from you, I'll invite you to speak. Mr. Visnjic, these are all points that go to the weight that would be attributable to evidence in due course. What you failed to do - and this is what I want to hear a submission about - is where the breach of the rule is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's one thing I'm certain of. In the statement given in June 2002, the witness went to the locations with an investigator. Now we heard from the witness that on that occasion certain photographs were taken. We haven't received any of those, and the witness stated that he showed the specific locations to the investigators, the locations where some things took place or the locations where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Most of the questions on that line led to answers which indicated that no photographs were taken. Identify for me the transcript pages and lines where he said otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 53; 22, 23, and 24, concerning two locations, Meca or Rakovina and Trnje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, where's the other one? Meca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was probably the first question. Page 52; 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, why can't you go to the Prosecution and ask for these?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I've only found out about it today. Do you think I should do it today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you establish a breach, if this turns out to be accurate, you can address it then. But at the moment the witness appears to be fairly vague except in relation to one photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so, but I wanted to state my position. In my view, those photographs should have come together with the statement from 2002, and they were supposed to have been disclosed at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, that's the extent of your submission, that there are these photographs apparently which you say have not been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Or perhaps they should have been submitted to us in accordance with Rule 68. I still don't know what's on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Moeller, can you address that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the investigator who went to the field with the witness in 2002 is still in house, and I haven't seen such photographs. We're inquiring and we will get back to the Defence and you about that as soon as I have a final response from him. We already initiated it. But I haven't seen any of these photographs in the system for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Neither have I seen any sketches or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How quickly can this be checked?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I hope in the course of today, Your Honours. We already sent an e-mail to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you make sure that the witness stays just in case something turns up?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that means that you should really report to the Trial Chamber later today what the outcome of this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have another witness that's available to put on today. Witness K14 was our next scheduled witness. Over the weekend I think we learned that she was having weather-related travel difficulties. She's arriving today. We have the witness Ambassador Petritsch who is being proofed today and we now will put him on tomorrow and do K14 after him, followed by Barayabar. We think those three, then, will fill up the rest of the week. I know I had an e-mail from your legal officer about addressing the issue regarding Mr. Coo tomorrow. I didn't know if you wanted to do that before Ambassador Petritsch starts or after, or what time you propose to address that. I think Mr. O'Sullivan was going to be the primary speaker for the Defence in that connection. I don't see him here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There were a number of other items mentioned in an e-mail that you sent, Mr. Hannis, but none of them seem to merit taking up court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour. I think those are matters for us to work together with the Defence on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, is there no question of us using the final session today to deal with Coo?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we were put on notice that it would happen only tomorrow, the submissions. Mr. O'Sullivan will be available tomorrow in the court for the submissions. And I told -- as I informed the Trial Chamber previously, he is in -- that it is his task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it now doesn't look as though it will be tomorrow. It's going to have to be at a later stage if the time is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Whatever pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I'm not sure -- I think that -- well, if my understanding was correct, perhaps the witness who testified just now, perhaps he could be re-called tomorrow. Perhaps his attention should be drawn to the fact that he is still under oath and that he should not contact anyone about any matters related to this case, if possible, if he hasn't left the building by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've already heard that he won't be leaving, and there's no need for these matters to be drawn to his attention because the only issue relates to photographs and not to his evidence in general. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just because we are dealing with this issue, just now we received the e-mail from the investigator Mr. Jonathan Sutch, who went on this mission when the addendum statement was taken, and he says that no photographs were taken when he went with him on this mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now I've really nothing to say. Now I have to give this some profound thought as to what I'm going to do next. But at any rate, I thank the OTP for their prompt reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think in the circumstances the witness can now be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I'm trying to fill up our time today, sort of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you certainly get the prize for that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sincerely hope so. Your Honour, I think that since we managed to check this so quickly with the photographs, and before the witness leaves, there is one very important thing that remains unclear to me: My learned friend Mr. Visnjic asked him whether the investigator asked him to indicate the location to him where these five women were buried and his answer was no. In his previous testimony he said that -- rather, in the additional information, I'm not sure now. I'm a bit out of focus after my cross-examination. But we were previously told that the investigator told him that there was no need to show anything. Now, what is true? Did the investigators of the Tribunal try to exhume the grave where these bodies are? And Mr. Stamp said publicly before this Court that he would not charge the accused with regard to that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought the position had been made clear yesterday that the witness did himself mark the grave but that no investigation was carried out to exhume the bodies or even, indeed, to find the grave. And I don't think he said otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I will find it in the additional examination, or perhaps my colleague Ms. Moeller, who is more familiar with this. It does say that in response to the question -- oh, yes, yes, I'll tell you now. I've just remembered. In response to Judge Kwon's question, in the last line of his testimony, on the last page of his testimony, as to whether he pointed out the place where it was that he buried the corpses, he answered that he had been told that there was no need for that; that they knew. And in the statement he just said that he threw away part of the engine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that he marked it by throwing part of the engine and he said that probably it went rusty by now. And he did not talk about that anywhere else except in the statement. 8324 is the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got it and you haven't -- we've had your questions, the questions you want to ask. What else do you want to do? You've had your opportunity, surely, to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to find out from the OTP investigator what it is that is true, whether he really told this witness that they knew already. Did they go to the location? Did they try to find the two bodies? Or did they perhaps try to find the bodies and did not manage to find them? We haven't got any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you can call the investigator if you wish in your Defence case if you want to contradict that statement. That's something for you to do when you're building your own defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but I thought that that was the obligation of the Prosecutor, to prove the existence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not understanding you, Mr. Bakrac. You've known about this all through the evidence of the witness. What is it you're saying has changed that leads to you now asking to do something unusual? Are you saying you just made a mistake in not asking him, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. I think that there is a difference between the answer that he gave to Mr. Visnjic and the answer that he gave to Mr. Kwon. Mr. Visnjic asked him, "Did you" -- rather, "Did the investigator ask you to take him to the place where the bodies were buried?" and he said no. And in this transcript, in my view, it's quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He said no. It's just the same. He gave an explanation in the transcript and that wasn't challenged by Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what he said, that he -- in the transcript in the previous trial. He said no because he already knew. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that didn't come out after you had cross-examined; that was something you knew about before you cross-examined. And there's no justification for an exceptional course here. All Mr. Visnjic got was confirmation of that answer without the explanation. And if you want to deal with it through the investigator and to lead him as a witness, that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you know how long Mr. O'Sullivan's submissions are likely to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is he on the end of an e-mail?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can send an e-mail to him, but it will probably take a couple of minutes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, but could you try to give us some guidance as quickly as possible and then we will communicate to you whether we will be hearing the witness first, which is most likely, or whether we'll allocate time tomorrow to hear this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. May I inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dawson --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Dawson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, in addition to the time that Mr. O'Sullivan will need, I can say on behalf of our Defence team that we are going to need seven, eight, or ten minutes in order to explain our position with regard to Coo as well. So from that point of view, it would be more expedient to start with Petritsch first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what else you planned for today, but I would have a brief proposal orally. I would like to deal with it within three or four minutes. Would it be more convenient to deal with it now or later? It doesn't have to do with Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we would normally have a break at this point, but you might find that others feel they could make better use of the day if we dealt with this some other way. Do you want to -- I mean, is it something that needs to be done today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It relates to a document, Your Honour, that we received from the OTP. I talked to Mr. Hannis about it and there is mutual agreement that we tender the document -- 3D515 is the document. It was disclosed. It's in the system. That would be my proposal. You can have a look at the document at any time and you can rule on that. Again, when we have a break between Prosecution witnesses yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider that. I understand that there are occasions when Mr. Hannis is content that a document that would normally only appear in the Defence case might nevertheless come in at this stage, and if it fits into that category without his objection, then, no doubt, that is likely to be approved. But give us an opportunity to consider the position. Mr. Hannis, you know I said last week that it's now going to become an increasing problem not to have any spare witnesses, especially when you're down to a very small number. I really think you ought to make some effort to overlap some of them so that we don't constantly come up with this problem. I say that -- make that comment because I think it's in the interests of justice that you use the full time available to present your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't want you to take the smile on my face to indicate that I take this lightly. I am ever mindful of your repeated admonitions about that. Sometimes I wake up at 3.00 in the morning thinking about it. We are down to our last 10 or 12 or 14 witnesses, depending on who shows up and certain rulings. We are trying to do our best, but among this group we have some internationals who are travelling sometimes across the ocean. We will make our best efforts, but we still are certain and confident that we'll finish with the evidence in this case by the 23rd of March, even though we may have another gap or two between now and the end. But we will do our best to have at least one or two back-ups standing by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that means we will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24
